questions.prompt: Answer: "Yassine visited his grandmother last Sunday." Ask about "last Sunday".

options.text: Where did Yassine visit his grandmother?
When did Yassine visit his grandmother?
When did Yassine visited his grandmother?

questions.explanation: "Last Sunday" is a time, so the question word is "when". The verb is in the past, so the helper is "did", and the main verb goes back to its base form: When did Yassine visit his grandmother? Keeping "visited" after "did" marks the past twice, and leaving out "did" forgets the helper.

questions.prompt: A note is worth ten dinars. Complete: "It is a ___ note."
questions.explanation: A number + noun makes a compound adjective, and in a compound adjective the noun stays singular: a ten-dinar note, like a five-dinar coin. "Ten-dinars" is the tempting mistake, because the value is ten dinars — but an adjective never takes a plural.

questions.prompt: Which sentence links the cause and the consequence correctly?

options.text: He didn't revise because he failed his test.
Because he didn't revise, so he failed his test.
He failed his test, so he didn't revise.
He didn't revise, so he failed his test.

questions.explanation: Not revising is the cause and failing the test is the consequence, so "so" stands in front of the consequence. With "because" in front of the failed test, the sentence turns the result into the cause, and "because… so…" uses two linkers for one link, a calque of Arabic, which can use both words in one sentence. Finally, "He failed his test, so he didn't revise" puts "so" in front of the cause.

questions.prompt: Complete: "The children decorated the classroom ___, with no help from the teacher."
questions.explanation: The subject is plural (the children), and the pronoun means "with no help", so the reflexive form is "themselves". "Theirselves" and "themself" are the tempting non-existent forms, and "them" would point to other people.

questions.prompt: Find the sentence with a mistake.

options.text: The cat is drinking its milk.

questions.explanation: The mistake is "our's": possessive pronouns (ours, yours, hers, theirs) never take an apostrophe, so the correct sentence is "These seats are ours." "Its milk" is right (its is the possessive adjective, with no apostrophe) and "Nadia's bag" is a correct genitive.

questions.prompt: Complete: "Before ___ (leave) the house, close all the windows."
questions.explanation: "Before" is a preposition, and after a preposition the verb takes the gerund. "Leave" ends in a silent e, which drops before -ing: leaving. "To leave" copies the French "avant de partir", and "leaveing" keeps the e.
